title: Chapter 162 – The Girl Who Did Not Speak
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Yue]

On the fourth morning after the first wake, the Hall loses a lamp.

It happens at the far end of the Annex corridor, where the ring of light curves out of sight, and Yue sees it only because she is looking for it. She has been looking for such things for days. A lamp that had burned gold for six hundred years goes pale, flickers, shrinks to a bead of orange, and then to nothing at all. There is no sound. In the place where it hung, the dark leans in.

She stands in the corridor with her palm flat against the wall and counts the stumbles. Thirty-eight an hour. Better than the worst, worse than the day before. The pulse of the Gate has the uneven sag of a heart that is tired of beating.

Nurse comes out of the Annex with a bowl of washed rags and sees her, and follows her gaze to the dark patch, and does not say anything. She only sets the bowl down on the floor and goes to the nearest unbroken lamp and carefully, with a long brass snuffer, puts it out.

Yue frowns. She writes on the slate.

Why?

"Because there are two hundred and sixty-three lamps left in this passage," says Nurse. "And the Hall can feed two hundred and sixty. I would rather choose which go dark than let the Hall choose for me."

How many do we have?

"Enough for the next wake. Not enough for the one after." Nurse straightens her apron. "The old man is awake and wishes to speak to you. Go to him. I will do the rest."

Yue looks at the dark patch a moment longer. Then she goes.

* * *

Lin Jian is sitting up.

It is the first time since the collapse, and Bell stands at the foot of the cot with her arms folded and the expression of a woman who has lost an argument and means to be gracious about it. He has a blanket round his shoulders. His face is the color of old paper. But his eyes are clear, and when Yue comes in, he lifts a hand and gestures to the stool.

"Sit," he says. "I have a favor to ask, and I would like you to be comfortable before you say no."

She sits. She takes the slate out of her sash.

"The next is Mo Yan." He says the name carefully, as if it were fragile. "Operator Six. Eight years old. She does not speak."

Why not?

"Ethan does not know." The corner of his mouth tightens. "She was not mute when she was taken. Her mother reported that she talked a great deal, in fact, from the age of one. After the copy, she stopped. The record says that the blur took her voice. I do not understand it. Ethan says it is the price the seal extracted from her, and that he never found a way to give it back."

Yue's chalk hovers.

"I would like you to be with her when she wakes. Not Bell. Not Nurse. You."

Because I am deaf?

"Because you will not talk at her." He meets her eyes. "Because you have lived in the silence, and know that it is a place, not an absence. She will be frightened. She will have been awake in her own mind for six hundred years, alone, with no voice and no one to hear her if she had one. I think you are the only person here who can sit in that room and not need her to say anything."

Yue looks at the slate. Her hand has begun to shake, and she lets it.

I can try, she writes.

"That is all I ask."

* * *

The wake is quieter than the others.

Mei is tiny now. She is the size of a seed, a pinpoint of bright pale light in Ethan's cupped palms, and the shaft around her has gone nearly dark. Yue does not go down to see it. She is told afterward, by Bell, in short strokes, that the girl spoke once, very briefly, to say she was ready, and nothing else. The cost reads fifteen percent. The Hall drops another lamp.

In the Annex, Yue sits on the floor beside the third cot with her back to the wall and her hands in her lap.

Mo Yan lies on her back with her mouth shut tight, even in sleep. Her face is turned toward the wall, the way it has been for six hundred years. She has a sharp, small, stubborn face, with straight brows and a stubborn jaw. Her hair is cut very short and her hands are curled under her chin like paws. Above the cot, pinned to the plaster, hangs the charcoal drawing: the house, the tree, the seven stick figures in a row.

The glow rises around her. The white ring turns. Yue feels the floor stumble under her and recover, and stumble again, and she breathes slowly, and watches.

There is no gasp. No cry. No wild gulp of air. Mo Yan wakes the way a cat wakes, all at once, with her eyes open and her body tight and her gaze going straight to the corners of the room.

She sits up.

She does not look at the ceiling. She does not look at the lamps. She looks at the door, then at the window, then at the faces in the room, one after another, with the narrow watchful stare of a child who has learned that it is safer to count the exits than to cry. Her eyes pass over Bell and over Nurse and over the two small boys huddled on the first cot. They come to Yue, sitting on the floor with her hands in her lap, and they stop.

Yue does not smile. She does not wave. She only lifts her open palm to her chest, slowly, and holds it there, and lets her face be still.

Mo Yan looks at her for a very long time.

Then, without a word, she slides off the cot, crosses the floor in her bare feet, and sits down next to Yue against the wall.

* * *

They sit that way for most of an hour.

Nobody speaks. Bell, with the instincts of a good midwife, has taken the two boys out into the corridor for broth and told Nurse to follow. The Annex is empty but for the two of them and the old man sleeping on the eighth cot and the white ring of the first bed, slowly fading. Yue can feel the child's shoulder against her arm. It is thin and hard and very warm, and it trembles, the smallest tremor, every few breaths.

She does not look at her. She looks straight ahead, at the opposite wall, and breathes in and out.

After a while Mo Yan reaches over and takes the slate out of Yue's lap.

She turns it in her hands. She runs her thumb over the smooth black surface, and over the ledge where the chalk lies, and Yue sees her eyes widen at the faint scrawl of old words that has not been quite wiped away. 31. Friend. Pebble. Mo Yan sets the slate down on her knees and looks at the chalk.

Then she shakes her head, quickly, and from somewhere inside her small pale smock she pulls a short stub of charcoal. She holds it up.

Yue nods.

Mo Yan turns, and on the plaster of the wall, beside the pinned drawing, she begins to draw.

She draws fast. Her hand moves in long confident strokes, the sleeve rucked up above her wrist, her small body bent close to the wall. A line, a curve, a shaded patch of black. Yue watches a shape unfold: a wide dark space, a thread of light running through it, and in the thread, small, tilted, a girl with her hand pressed flat to a floor. It is her. It is exactly her. The jut of the chin, the knotted braid, the stiff set of the shoulders. In a dozen strokes the charcoal has caught her better than a mirror would.

She stares at it. Her throat is tight.

Mo Yan steps back. She looks at the drawing, and at Yue, and then she points at the girl in the picture's hand, flat on the floor, and at Yue's own hand, and she raises both eyebrows in a question.

How did you know? Yue thinks. She has not told anyone, not in this room. She has not written it.

She lifts her own palm and presses it to the floor, and nods.

And Mo Yan smiles. It is a small, crooked, delighted smile, the first Yue has seen on her face, and it changes everything about it.

* * *

By the afternoon Mo Yan is drawing the Seam.

She does it on the wall of the Annex, by the stove, with the charcoal stub worn to a nub. Yue watches from the cot. The drawing begins as a long jagged line, running the width of the plaster from left to right, and then, below it, a great many small marks, dense and dark and crowding, the way ants crowd at the mouth of a nest. She shades them heavily. She leaves a gap in the line at the center, a patch of white, and in the gap she draws a tiny round house with a lamp in the window.

The Hall.

Then she goes back to the left edge of the wall and draws something else: a spiral, narrow at the bottom, widening as it climbs. At the lowest end she puts a dot. At each turn she puts another dot, closer together. At the top, just under the house, she presses the charcoal so hard that it snaps.

Ao has crept up to watch. He tugs Yue's sleeve and points at the dots and holds up fingers, slowly, one by one, and she follows his lips as he counts. Thirty-one. Thirty-one days, perhaps, before the first of them reach the house.

Not sixty, Yue writes.

Ao shakes his head. His small face is grave. Sixty to the Wall, he says. Thirty-one to here.

She looks at the broken charcoal on the floor. She looks at the dots, crowded close under the tiny house.

She does not tell Bell. Not yet. She puts the slate down and sits with her back to the plaster and lets the child at her side settle against her arm.

* * *

The two small boys are, at first, merely suspicious of the girl.

Ao and Tao hover at the doorway of the Annex with the rabbit and the top clutched to their chests. Mo Yan, standing by the third cot, watches them with the narrow stillness of a cat that has been introduced to two dogs. For several minutes nobody moves. Then Tao announces, loudly, that he has a top, and spins it on the floor between them.

It whirs. It wobbles. It slows, and tips.

Mo Yan crouches. She picks up her stub of charcoal. On the floorboards, next to the fallen top, she draws a small wobbling circle, and under it a smaller one, and under that a smaller one still, and shows with her hand how they get smaller, and smaller, and fall.

Tao stares.

"That's exactly what it does," he says.

Mo Yan nods, satisfied. She hands him the charcoal.

Within a quarter of an hour the floor of the Annex is covered with drawings. A rabbit with a scarf. A top with rays coming off it. A stove with a ridiculous face. Ao, lying flat on his stomach with his tongue between his teeth, adds a very large and very lopsided duck. The three of them are shrieking with laughter, and Yue, on the cot, cannot hear any of it. But she feels it, a rippling joy that travels along the boards into her bones, and she holds still and lets it come.

Nurse, at the door, is wiping her eyes with her apron.

* * *

Mei speaks to them that evening, through the grille.

Her voice is very small now. It has the clear light quality of a bell heard from a long way off. Bell relays it to Yue in a quick scrawl, one line at a time, and Yue reads it with her chin in her fist.

Hello, Mo Yan, says Mei. You don't have to answer. I just wanted to say I'm glad you're awake.

The child at Yue's side goes rigid. She looks at the grille. Then, slowly, she lifts her charcoal and draws on the wall a little round face with a mouth that curves up.

Thank you, says Mei. That's a good smile. Mine is smaller now, but I'll try to match it.

Mo Yan draws another face, lower down, with large dark eyes. A question mark floats above it.

I'm tired, says Mei, simply. But I'm all right. I'd rather be tired and useful than rested and hiding. A silence. Ethan says you could always hear the Hall. Is that true?

Mo Yan's hand pauses.

He says you drew it, when you were small. The sound of the Gate. He kept the pictures. He said they were the first thing that told him how the pulse behaved. The voice has gone soft. You never told anyone how you knew. But I think I understand. I think you didn't talk because you were listening.

The charcoal drops from Mo Yan's fingers. Yue has not read the words aloud, but she sees the child's face as she hears them, and it is as if a hand has reached into her and turned a key.

She makes a sound. Yue feels it, more than hears it: a tiny, cracked vibration in the shoulder against her arm, a hum that starts at the back of the throat and goes nowhere, the first sound that has come from that small body in six hundred years.

It is not a word. But it is a start.

* * *

Bell takes the news with a quiet nod and says, bluntly, that the child will need rest, and warm food, and no more shocks for at least two days.

Yue agrees. But she cannot sleep.

She sits against the wall in the dark Annex with the sleeping children breathing around her and her hand flat on the floor, and she listens, as she has learned to do, to the long slow pulse of the Hall. She is aware of Mo Yan beside her, curled on her side with the stub of charcoal in her fist, and of the small warmth of the body. After a time she realizes that she can feel the child's hum.

It is faint. But it is there, a thread in the pulse, like a note held under the big slow song of the Gate. A single pure tone, rising and falling in time with the child's breath.

She puts her other hand on the child's back.

The tone gets louder. Not in her ears; she has no ears for it. It gets louder in her palms, her forearms, her ribs. It moves into her sternum, into the little dent where the pebble used to sit, and settles there like a bird. And behind it comes something she has not felt in a very long time.

Shape.

It is not a sound. It is the idea of a sound. A wavering line, silver and thin, drawn against a dark ground. She cannot name the pitch. She cannot say how she knows it. But the line is there, in the place where her hearing used to be, and it rises and falls, rises and falls, in a rhythm that is as plain to her as a face.

She holds very still. She does not dare breathe.

The line wavers. It steadies. And through the child's hand, which has crept into hers in her sleep, Yue feels a word.

* * *

Ethan asks for Yue in the small hours.

She does not hear him ask. Bell wakes her with a hand on the shoulder and a lamp held low, and writes on the slate, He wants you at the grille. Alone. He says it is about the girl. Yue pulls her cloak on over her smock and follows the lamp down the corridor, past the dark patches where the lamps have failed, to the little round room where the wall opens on the shaft.

The grille is cold. She presses her forehead to the metal, as Bell showed her, and lets the vibration of the voice come through the bone.

It is not words. It is only a low uneven shaking, a man trying to speak steadily. She waits. After a while Bell, standing behind her, begins to write on the slate, one line at a time, lifting each for her to read.

I wanted to ask a favor. I cannot ask it of Jian. He has given too much. I cannot ask it of Bell. She has to keep him alive.

You are the only one left who can sit with a child and not be afraid of her silence.

I think Mo Yan is going to ask you for something. She has asked everyone for it, in her way, for six hundred years. She wants to be heard.

I want you to be careful. She is eight, and she is clever, and she will give you everything she has, because she has never had anyone to give it to. Whatever she gives, it will cost her. The copy exacts a price for every use. If you take too much, you may take what is left.

Yue reads it twice. She writes, with the chalk, What is left?

A long pause. Bell turns the slate over and writes the answer.

I do not know. That is why I am afraid.

* * *

She tells Bell in the morning, in a rush, with the slate jammed against her chest.

I felt her hum. Through her skin. And I saw it. Not with my eyes.

Bell frowns and takes the slate and reads it twice. "You saw it?"

Like a drawing. A line, in my head. It went up and down. When she breathed out, it went down. She is writing fast, too fast. Then she held my hand and there was something else. I think it was her name for me.

"Her name for you."

A shape. I don't know how to describe it. She stops, and sets her jaw, and begins again. It was like a little bell. A small one, with a crack in it.

Bell looks at her for a long moment. Then she says, "Come with me."

They find Lin Jian where they left him, propped on the cot with the blanket round his shoulders and a bowl of rice gruel on his knees. He listens while Yue writes it all out again, slowly, in careful strokes, and when she has finished he sets the bowl on the sill and sits with his hands folded.

"Tell me what you felt," he says. "When she hummed."

Her breath. Her pulse. A tone, I think. It was thin.

"And the shape of her name for you?"

A bell with a crack.

He closes his eyes. The silence stretches. "Ethan says the Operators are conduits," he says at last. "The copy is a kind of channel. Each of them carries something the others do not. Mine is the panel. Ao carries the stored message. And Mo Yan..." He opens his eyes. "I think Mo Yan carries the sound. Not the voice. The sound itself, the shape of it, the part under the words."

She can't speak.

"She does not need to. She is a listener, Yue. She hears the Hall, the Gate, the beasts under the Seam. And if she can hear them, then perhaps she can hear you."

Yue stares at him.

"I do not know what it would cost," he says gently. "But I think you should ask her."

* * *

She asks her at noon, on the floor of the Annex, with the slate on her knee and a stub of charcoal on the boards between them.

Can you hear what I think?

Mo Yan reads it upside down, then right side up. She tilts her head. She picks up the charcoal, hesitates, and draws a small round ear with a spiral inside. Beside it she draws a hand, and between the two she draws a short wavering line.

Through touch? Yue writes.

Mo Yan nods. She holds out her left hand, palm up.

Yue puts her own hand in it.

The child's skin is dry and warm. Her grip is steady. For a few breaths nothing happens, and then Yue feels the thin silver line rise in her mind, and she closes her eyes. The line is a little wider than before. It has color now: a faint pearl-gray. It shivers.

I can hear you, Yue thinks, as clearly as she can. Can you hear me?

The line thickens. It folds on itself, once, and a new shape forms in the dark behind her eyes: a small, tilted, unmistakable bell with a crack in its side, ringing.

And inside the ringing, so softly that she almost loses it, there is a voice.

It is not a voice, exactly. It is the idea of one: high, light, crooked, a child's voice that has never been used. It does not say words. It says her name.

Yue.

She opens her eyes. Mo Yan is looking at her with an expression of absolute solemn delight. Her mouth is shut. Her charcoal-black fingers are tight in Yue's. And in the quiet that has lived in Yue's skull for forty-three days, the child's silent voice rings out, clear and bright, like a bell struck at last.

Yue, says Mo Yan. Yue. Yue. Yue.

Then Yue sees the dark bead gather at the child's nostril.

It is a single drop, slow and bright against the pale skin, and Mo Yan does not notice it. She is laughing, without sound, her whole small body shaking with it, and the drop falls onto the back of her hand and spreads.

Yue's stomach drops. She tries to pull her hand away. The child's grip tightens at once, fierce, and the bell rings again in her skull, high and stubborn. No, it says, without a word. No. Stay.

You are bleeding, Yue thinks, as hard as she can.

I know. The reply comes not in words but in a shape, a little crooked smile drawn in silver. It is a small price.

It is not small.

It is smaller than the quiet.

Yue holds the child's hand and weighs it. Behind them, on the eighth cot, Lin Jian is awake and watching, and his face is grave. Beside him Bell has half risen, her lips parted, and Yue sees her decide, after a long moment, to say nothing. The healer sinks back to her stool.

She counts, in her head, as she does with the stumbles. Nine breaths. Ten. At the twelfth the child's grip loosens, just a little, and the silver line wavers. Mo Yan lets go. She wipes her nose on her wrist, looks at the red smear with mild interest, and then goes to the wall and draws a very small drop with a very large frown over it.

Later, says the drawing, plainly. Later, we try again.

Yue nods. She wipes her own eyes with the heel of her hand. She has heard one name, in a bell with a crack in it, in a place where she thought there was nothing at all. She will pay anything for the next one. She knows that, and she knows that it frightens her.

She begins to cry again, and does not try to stop.
